text: A multi-agent research system substantially outperforms a single agent using the same frontier model on an internal breadth-heavy research evaluation (Anthropic reports ~90% improvement).
note: Anthropic primary source reports +90.2% on an internal research eval (not public, not compute-matched: multi-agent uses ~3.75x the tokens of single agent, per exp1). Contradicting evidence (Tran & Kiela 2026; equal-cost preprint 2609.04217) concerns compute-matched settings on other tasks, so it does not refute the reported number but undercuts attributing it to architecture; Kim et al. show +80.8% gains on decomposable tasks, consistent with breadth-heavy research benefiting.

text: Agentic deep-research systems score far higher than the same vendor's single non-agentic models on hard public benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam and BrowseComp.
note: Vendor primary sources: BrowseComp Deep Research 51.5% vs o1 9.9% / GPT-4o w/ browsing 1.9%; HLE 26.6% vs o3-mini-high 13.0%. Caveats: vendor-run, agent has tools the baselines lack, HLE baselines partly on text-only subset; DeepTRACE shows deep research outputs still contain many unsupported statements (context, not refutation).

text: Most of the measured advantage of research agents is explained by extra compute/token spend and tool access rather than by agent architecture per se; equal-budget comparisons are rarely reported.
note: Anthropic: token usage alone explains 80% of BrowseComp variance; BrowseComp paper: performance scales smoothly with test-time compute; Tran & Kiela: MAS advantages better explained by unaccounted computation; equal-cost preprint finds no significant MAS benefit. 'Most' is an inference from variance decomposition and a few compute-matched studies, not a direct measurement on frontier deep-research systems; one cited preprint (2609.04217) is unreviewed. Counter-search found no compute-matched study showing architecture gains on hard research tasks.

text: When cost is controlled, simple baselines (single model with retries/sampling) can match or beat complex agent systems on some benchmarks.
note: AI Agents That Matter: SOTA HumanEval agents do not outperform simple baselines, escalation beats LDB at <half cost; Agentless beat open-source SWE agents at $0.70; Tran & Kiela: single agent matches/beats MAS at equal thinking tokens. Evidence is from coding and multi-hop QA, older-generation systems; 'some benchmarks' scope is deliberately narrow. Kim et al. note coordination returns diminish as single-agent baselines strengthen.

text: On long-horizon difficult research-engineering tasks, autonomous agents still underperform skilled humans given larger time budgets, limiting claims of autonomous superiority.
note: RE-Bench: agents 4x humans at 2h but humans narrowly ahead at 8h and 2x at 32h; PaperBench: best agent 21.0% replication, models do not outperform ML PhD baseline. The contradicting 2h result is resolved by time budget: agents win short horizons, humans win longer ones. Results date from 2024-2025 models and may be outdated by newer agents.

text: Multi-agent LLM systems often show only minimal gains over single-agent baselines and fail in systematic ways.
note: MAST: MAS gains on popular benchmarks often minimal; 14 failure modes across 1600+ traces in 7 frameworks; Kim et al.: -70% on sequential planning. Contradicting +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning (Kim et al.) shows gains are task-dependent, not absent; claim says 'often', which both results are consistent with.
